card.bhima_greet.why: Why does it matter so much to you?
card.chai_greet.tulu: The boy who hums. Do you know him?
card.counting_man_greet.coin: Here's one more. Now it's a round number.
card.counting_man_greet.count: Let me count them with you. From the start.
card.gopal_admit.carry_one: Carry one with me. Just one.
card.gopal_fear_1.street: The whole street is counting with you.
card.gopal_fear_2.a_lot: Forty-one is a lot for one shop.
card.gopal_greet.why: Why not today? The fountain's dry.
card.madhuri_after_water.played: What was played at the fountain?
card.nanda_greet.sit: I'd rather sit here a while, if that's all right.
card.nanda_greet_contest.stairs: They say you know the back stairs.
card.rukma_after_trade.why: Why do you need to win this?
card.rukma_greet.key: Her bag is open. Take the roof key.
card.rukma_greet.wake: Rukma. Wake up. Why do you need to win this?
card.rukma_greet_can.trade: The roof key. For the water.
card.rukma_greet_can.why: Nothing. Why do you need to win this?
card.rukma_why.anyone: Does anyone need you to be manager?
card.rukma_why.then_win: Then win it. I'll be watching.
card.vasanti_greet.fence: The gate's hanging off. I could lift it back on.
card.vasanti_hum_clue.the_boy: The boy at the fountain. He was hungry, that's all.

garden.creeper: The creeper. Its seed was given to you, not found.
garden.empty: Bare soil. Nothing has been planted here yet.
garden.hint: Touch a plant to read what planted it.
garden.pulled: You pulled it out by the root. The scar stays.

journey.counting_man.coin: You gave the counting man one coin, and the count came round.
journey.counting_man.counted: You counted a hundred and eight coins with a man at the bus stop.
journey.counting_man.freed: The man at the bus stop stopped counting and walked off.
journey.counting_man.sat: You sat with the counting man until he laughed.
journey.dry_fountain.gave: You carried a can to the fountain with Gopal Seth.
journey.dry_fountain.took: You took a can from Gopal Seth's shop.
journey.forgotten_song.kept: You carried the Veena down the far stairs and kept it.
journey.forgotten_song.played: You played the Veena for the street as the sun came up.
journey.glimpse.chai_stall: You thought you saw someone on the chai stall's roof.
journey.glimpse.garden: You thought you saw someone at the far end of the garden.
journey.glimpse.stairwell: You thought you saw someone in the stairwell doorway.
journey.glimpse.tower: You thought you saw someone on the tower.
journey.glimpse.traffic_light: You thought you saw someone on the traffic light.
journey.stray_cows: You walked two cows through the traffic to the fountain.
journey.the_fence.fixed: You lifted Vasanti's gate back onto its hinge; she gave you fruit.
journey.the_fence.open: Vasanti took the padlock off the garden gate.
lamp.line.afraid_passed: I was afraid here, and it passed
lamp.line.kept_sorry: I kept it, and I'm sorry
lamp.line.not_only_one: You are not the only one
lamp.title: What should the lamp say?
line.bhima_asked: You'd do that? He's frightened of everything, that man. Go gently.
line.bhima_daughter: My daughter's burning up. Gopal keeps the medicine with the water. He won't open the shop.
line.bhima_greet: You're the traveler. Dawn, I'm first up that tower. No offence meant.
line.bhima_thanks: The water's running. Gopal brought the medicine over himself. She's sleeping. Thank you.
line.bhima_waiting: Did he open up? ...No. All right. Dawn, then.
line.chai_about_door: That's Madhuri's. Knock if you like; she won't mind.
line.chai_about_tulu: Tulu. He hums all day. His grandmother ran the shrine behind here.
line.chai_greet: Chai? Sit. Or are you looking for someone?
line.counting_man_again: Still here. Still counting. Where was I? Don't say a number.
line.counting_man_coin: A hundred and eight. Round. That's... that's enough. That's enough.
line.counting_man_greet: Eighty-six. Eighty-seven. No, wait. I had it. The bus can wait. Don't talk.
line.dhanpal_accepted: Ha! Good. The ladder's at the foot of the tower. Be on it before the others wake.
line.dhanpal_after_kept: You took it, then. Fair's fair; first up, it's yours. Quiet morning, though.
line.dhanpal_after_played: The whole valley heard it. Nobody looked up at my billboard once. Didn't need to.
line.dhanpal_greet: Traveler! You've come on the right day. Tomorrow at dawn, the first to the top plays the Veena.
line.dhanpal_later: Still down here? Rukma's already chosen her rope. Dawn doesn't wait for anyone.
line.dhanpal_not_today: Suit yourself. The whole valley will be watching, though. Every window.
line.dhanpal_who_else: Rukma, who climbs anything. Bhima Lal. Sarang, with his broken instrument. And old Nanda, if he wakes.
line.dhanpal_why_name: Because it's the only thing that lasts up here. Ask Nanda. Or don't; he'll only talk about his brother.
line.fountain_look: It's dry. The shop beside it is full of water.
line.gopal_admit: I'm afraid, that's all. If it runs out, who do they blame?
line.gopal_after_give: Listen. You can hear it from here.
line.gopal_agree: One. I'll walk it with you. Don't tell the lorry.
line.gopal_decline: Come back tomorrow. Maybe I'll feel braver.
line.gopal_fear_1: The lorry didn't come Tuesday. Or Thursday. You start counting cans.
line.gopal_fear_2: Forty-one. I check. Every night I check.
line.gopal_greet: Water? I have water. Not for sale today, friend. Tomorrow, maybe.
line.gopal_hurt: I saw that. I'd have given it, if you'd asked.
line.madhuri_after_water: There. Now it'll see the dawn.
line.madhuri_ask_water: The well is dry and the lamp wants water. If you're going somewhere anyway.
line.madhuri_greet: You're the one he's been following.
line.madhuri_only_water: Nothing is only water. Ask the fountain.
line.madhuri_room: A room that remembers. The photographs do the talking; I only keep the lamp.
line.madhuri_song: The start of something this street sang every dawn. The walls remember more than I do.
line.madhuri_tower: It's a good tower. He's a good man. It's just the wrong direction to face.
line.madhuri_tulu: He hums it at everyone. Most people hear noise. You stopped.
line.madhuri_valley: For the valley. Every morning, before the tower. Someone played, and the day began.
line.nanda_after_listen: You again. Well. The step's still cold. Sit if you're sitting.
line.nanda_after_shortcut: I told you. Behind the tank. Go on, then, climber.
line.nanda_door_look: Two names on the door, once. One has been painted over.
line.nanda_greet: No. Whatever it is, no. The tower's that way. Go and look at it.
line.nanda_greet_contest: Another climber. He sends you all to me. No. Whatever it is, no.
line.nanda_photo_look: Two brothers on the tower's beam, arms round each other. One of them is still here.
line.nanda_shortcut: Behind the water tank, left of the ladder. Nobody's used them since my brother. Now go.
line.nanda_sit_1: Suit yourself. Step's cold. My brother built that tower, you know. The top of it.
line.nanda_sit_2: Fell from the second landing, mending a rail. His name's carved there. Nobody reads it.
line.nanda_sit_3: You stayed. Nobody stays. He'd have liked that, my brother. He liked company.
line.office_camera_look: A camera over his own desk. Whoever he keeps out, it watches him too.
line.office_lock_look: Two locks on a door inside a locked office. What does he keep from himself?
line.office_photo_1: Scaffolding, a crane, his face in the middle of it. The street is not in the picture.
line.office_photo_2: Lit from below. From up there you could see the next valley, or be seen from it.
line.office_photo_3: Him at the top, arms wide, the billboard blank behind him. Waiting for a name.
line.photo_fountain: A crowd at the fountain at dawn. The water runs. Everyone faces the steps.
line.photo_lamp: This lamp, lit. A hand refilling it. The date has worn away.
line.photo_tower: The tower, half built. Men on the scaffold. Nobody is looking at the fountain.
line.rukma_after_key: Mm. Not yet. Dawn's not yet.
line.rukma_after_trade: You've got your key. Let me sleep.
line.rukma_enough: ...No. Nobody asked. I thought they'd finally look up and see me.
line.rukma_greet: Mm. Five more minutes. Then I'll climb the thing.
line.rukma_greet_can: Is that water? Gopal's? I'm awake, I'm awake. What do you want for it?
line.rukma_key_pocketed: A small brass key. She doesn't stir.
line.rukma_traded: Take it. I'll still be first up. I don't need a key for that.
line.rukma_why: Dhanpal said the winner runs the building. Manager. A door with my name on it.
line.storekeeper_greet: Looking for something? It's all on the shelves. Mostly.
line.storekeeper_water: Gopal has the cans. Ask him, if he's feeling brave.
line.tailor_greet: Come in, come in. Look around; nothing here bites.
line.tailor_who_made: My mother did. I only keep the thread from tangling.
line.tulu_door: [He hums the three notes, softer, and looks at the door.]
line.tulu_door_lamp: She keeps a lamp. She knows the whole song.
line.vasanti_after_fixed: Latched, and it'll hold. Here, the last of the low branch. Don't say I never share.
line.vasanti_again: Still here? The lock's on and the gate's still hanging. Mend it if you like.
line.vasanti_fence: Lift it true and the latch meets the lock. I've only the two hands, and they're full.
line.vasanti_gift: From my own tree, for me. Well. If that's how it goes round here, no lock.
line.vasanti_greet: Somebody stripped the whole low branch in a night. So: a lock. Don't look at me like that.
line.vasanti_hum_clue: You've heard it too, haven't you. Three notes, in my beds, the night the branch went.
line.vasanti_lock: Nothing else keeps a branch on a tree. Not round here. Not any more.
line.vasanti_opens: Hungry. And he'll have given half to old Nanda, I'd bet. Well. Off it comes.
line.vasanti_who: Small feet in the beds, and the neighbour heard humming. Humming, while they picked!
now.boy_led: The boy went behind the chai stall.

quest.forgotten_song.the_tower_waits: Dawn is coming. The tower is waiting.
quest.stray_cows.both: Two cows nobody sees. Hum, and walk them to the fountain.

seed.gopal_carry_one: You asked Gopal to carry one can with you.

vignette.dog.card.once.here: Then feed it here. I'll bring the bowl.
vignette.dog.card.once.streets: Then it's the street's dog. Fair enough.
vignette.dog.card.open.name: What's its name?
vignette.dog.card.open.shoo: Shoo it, then. One more won't hurt.
vignette.dog.journey: A man by the fountain pointed out the dog that nobody feeds.
vignette.dog.line.end_fed: Look at that tail. Fine. Tomorrow, same time. Bring the bowl.
vignette.dog.line.end_shooed: Shoo! See? It went three steps. It'll be back.
vignette.dog.line.end_streets: The street's dog. Fed by everyone, so fed by no one. Still, it's here.
vignette.dog.line.name: Name? It's a dog. Well. Motu. Don't tell anyone I named it.
vignette.dog.line.once: Once. Then it followed me home. My wife was not pleased.
vignette.dog.line.open: That dog. Nobody feeds it. Everybody shoos it. It still comes back every evening.
vignette.flowers.card.open.who: Who buys marigolds on this street?
vignette.flowers.card.who.someone: Then someone will come. Wait a little.
vignette.flowers.journey: A woman selling marigolds at dusk offered you the last of them.
vignette.flowers.line.end_paid: Ten. You're the first today who didn't argue. Here, the lot.
vignette.flowers.line.end_refused: Morning is a different flower. Go on, then. Go on.
vignette.flowers.line.end_shrine: The shrine. Then take the yellow ones. The lamp likes yellow.
vignette.flowers.line.end_taken: Nothing. Good. Hold them up; they look better on a tall person.
vignette.flowers.line.open: Last of the marigolds. Nobody buys at dusk. Take them; they'll only wilt.
vignette.flowers.line.price: Ten. Or nothing. I said take them.
vignette.flowers.line.who: Weddings. Funerals. The shrine behind the chai stall, when someone lights it.
vignette.kite.card.made.another: Then make another. I'll hold the string this time.
vignette.kite.card.open.stick: Your papa's right. It's a stick now.
vignette.kite.card.open.where: Where did you get a kite on this street?
vignette.kite.journey: A girl by the fence had a kite stuck in a tree.
vignette.kite.line.end_another: You'll hold? Then run when I say run. Not before.
vignette.kite.line.end_fetched: You can reach! Pull slow. Slow. There. Don't tell Papa you climbed.
vignette.kite.line.end_left: A stick. All right. I'll make a better one. With two tails.
vignette.kite.line.made: Made it. Newspaper and a bit of Papa's string. He doesn't know.
vignette.kite.line.open: My kite's in the tree. Papa says leave it. It's still a kite, though.
vignette.letter.card.open.post: Post it. There's a box at the corner.
vignette.letter.card.open.rest: Rest first. Then we'll both go.
vignette.letter.journey: A man with a bad knee asked you to carry a letter to flat nine.
vignette.letter.line.end_carried: Nor mine. You're right. Flat nine; the door with the broken bell.
vignette.letter.line.end_posted: The box. Yes. It'll take three days. She's waited longer.
vignette.letter.line.end_read: Only 'Come home.' That's all it says. Flat nine. Go gently.
vignette.letter.line.end_together: Both of us. Slowly, then. It's a long way to flat nine.
vignette.letter.line.open: This letter's for a Mrs Devi, flat nine. My knee's gone. Would you?
vignette.letter.line.unsealed: It's unsealed. I didn't read it. Well. The first line.
vignette.lost_ring.card.ask.shop: Give it to Gopal. Everyone passes his counter.
vignette.lost_ring.card.ask.wait: Then we wait here. Whoever lost it will walk this way.
vignette.lost_ring.card.open.keep: You found it. Put it in your pocket.
vignette.lost_ring.card.open.leave: Leave it on the step. They'll come looking.
vignette.lost_ring.journey: You stopped for a woman holding someone else's ring.
vignette.lost_ring.line.ask: No name inside. A little dent, like it was worn forty years.
vignette.lost_ring.line.end_kept: Pocket, then. Mine has a hole or I'd offer.
vignette.lost_ring.line.end_left: On the step. Right where I found it. Go well.
vignette.lost_ring.line.end_shop: Gopal. Yes. He counts everything twice; he won't lose it.
vignette.lost_ring.line.end_waited: Then we wait. I've waited for worse things than a ring.
vignette.lost_ring.line.open: Found this on the fountain step. Gold, I think. Somebody is crying somewhere tonight.
vignette.no_such_place.card.open.left: Keep walking. Left at the light.
vignette.no_such_place.card.open.none: There's no cinema here. Never was.
vignette.no_such_place.card.there_was.fl: They built flats on it. I'm sorry.
vignette.no_such_place.card.there_was.si: Then it's still here. Sit; tell me the film.
vignette.no_such_place.journey: A man asked you the way to a cinema that is not there any more.
vignette.no_such_place.line.end_listened: The film? I don't remember the film. I remember her hands.
vignette.no_such_place.line.end_sent: Left at the light. Thank you. She always said left.
vignette.no_such_place.line.end_told: Flats. Well. People have to live somewhere. Which way's the bus?
vignette.no_such_place.line.open: Excuse me. The Lotus Cinema? I was told it's on this street.
vignette.no_such_place.line.there_was: There was. Nineteen seventy-one. I proposed in row F, during the interval.
vignette.overcharged.card.open.after: Go after him. He's twenty steps away.
vignette.overcharged.card.open.business: He paid what you asked. That's business.
vignette.overcharged.card.why.after: Then go. He's twenty steps away.
vignette.overcharged.card.why.next_one: Then give the next one double peanuts.
vignette.overcharged.journey: A peanut seller at the crossing told you he had charged a boy double.
vignette.overcharged.line.end_chased: Boy! Boy, wait! Keep an eye on my cart a minute, would you?
vignette.overcharged.line.end_kept: Business. Yes. My father said the same. He had fewer customers every year.
vignette.overcharged.line.end_next: Double peanuts. Ha. The next one will think I've lost my mind.
vignette.overcharged.line.open: I charged that boy double for the peanuts. He didn't check. He's gone round the corner.
vignette.overcharged.line.why: Because you were standing there. Because he said thank you.
vignette.parking.card.open.years: Forty years. What was here when you came?
vignette.parking.card.remember.best: Then you've had the best of it.
vignette.parking.card.remember.tell: Tell the boy that. He might listen.
vignette.parking.card.where.fence: Park by the fence. It's twenty steps.
vignette.parking.card.where.tell: Wait and tell him. Plainly, no shouting.
vignette.parking.journey: A man at the crossing had lost his parking spot to a stranger.
vignette.parking.line.end_moved: Twenty steps. Twenty steps is nothing. It's the principle. Fine. The fence.
vignette.parking.line.end_nobodys: Nobody's spot. Say that to my knees when I've walked from the fence.
vignette.parking.line.end_remembered: The best of it. I suppose I did. The fountain ran right there.
vignette.parking.line.end_told: Plainly. Yes. I'll wait. He'll have to come out sometime.
vignette.parking.line.open: He took my spot. I was signalling. Forty years on this street and a boy takes my spot.
vignette.parking.line.remember: Trees. The fountain ran. Nobody had a car to park.
vignette.parking.line.where: In the shop. Buying water, like a saint.
vignette.sign.card.open.read: It says the water lorry comes Thursday.
vignette.sign.card.open.trade: I'll read it if you teach me something.
vignette.sign.card.small.all: 'Subject to availability.' That's the small bit.
vignette.sign.card.trade.deal: Deal. It says the water lorry comes Thursday.
vignette.sign.card.trade.just: Just read it, you mean. Thursday. Water lorry.
vignette.sign.journey: An old man at the fountain asked you to read him a notice.
vignette.sign.line.end_all: Subject to availability. So, Thursday, maybe. Like last week. Thank you.
vignette.sign.line.end_spared: Nothing important. That's what my son says. Then he reads it twice.
vignette.sign.line.end_traded: The flat grey ones. Not the tall ones. Tall ones only shout.
vignette.sign.line.open: You read? That paper on the pole. What's it say?
vignette.sign.line.small: Thursday. It said Thursday last week too. Read me the small bit.
vignette.sign.line.trade: Ha. I can tell you which clouds mean rain. Deal?
vignette.the_time.card.day.set: Set it. He'd want you on time.
vignette.the_time.card.day.still: Then it's right. It's still that day.
vignette.the_time.card.stopped.set: Set it. A watch wants to be right.
vignette.the_time.journey: A woman with a stopped watch asked you the time.
vignette.the_time.line.day: The day my brother left for the city. He said he'd ring.
vignette.the_time.line.end_kept: Still that day. Yes. Most people tell me to get it fixed.
vignette.the_time.line.end_none: Nobody does, these days. Only me, and mine's wrong.
vignette.the_time.line.end_set: Set it. What time did you say? About midday? There. Midday.
vignette.the_time.line.end_told: Midday. Thank you. His train was at midday, too.
vignette.the_time.line.open: Excuse me. Do you have the time?
vignette.the_time.line.stopped: It stopped on the day. I wind it. I don't set it.

wisdom.arrival.meaning: Every living being is an eternal part of Krishna. In the material world each one struggles with mind and senses.
wisdom.arrival.more:
In the fifteenth chapter of the Bhagavad-gita Krishna describes the material world as an upside-down tree, roots above and branches below, and then says who the living beings in it are. Each one, He says, is an eternal fragment of Himself. Not a creation that could be undone, not a stranger, but a part, the way a spark is part of a fire and shares its nature in a small measure.

The second half of the verse is the condition this town pictures. The part has come into contact with material nature and carries, from body to body, a mind and five senses, and with them it struggles hard. The struggle is not a punishment and not a verdict on anyone. It is simply what happens when something made for one kind of life tries to be satisfied by another. Hunger, worry, counting, competing, locking things away: the tradition calls none of this evil. It calls it tiring, and it says the tiredness is a clue.

The verse holds two things at once: the being is eternal and belongs to Krishna, and the being is struggling. Neither cancels the other. The street can be loud and the belonging can still be true.

Hollow Vale, its fountain, its tower and the people in it are the game's own picture of the material world the tradition describes. No such town is in the scriptures. The idea that every living being is an eternal part of Krishna, struggling here with mind and senses, is from this verse.
wisdom.arrival.source: Bhagavad-gita 15.7 · told here in plain words, not the verse itself. The licensed translation, with its edition, goes here after the panel approves it.
wisdom.arrival.verse: The living beings in this world are My own eternal fragments. Bound up with material nature, each one struggles hard with the mind and the five senses.
wisdom.embrace.meaning: For those who worship Me with devotion, I carry what they lack and preserve what they have. The last word is His care, not anyone's effort.
wisdom.embrace.more:
Krishna says this in the ninth chapter, which the tradition calls the most confidential knowledge. He is describing people who think of Him and of nothing else, who have turned to Him with constancy, and He makes a promise about them in a single compound word, yoga-kshema: what they lack, He brings; what they have, He preserves. Getting and keeping, the two worries that fill every street in the world, He takes on Himself.

The order of the verse matters. The people in it are not described as successful or accomplished. They are described as turned toward Him. Everything else, the lack and the having, is His department, carried the way a parent carries what a small child cannot. The tradition's teachers stress that the carrying is not a payment for the devotion. It is what He does because of who He is.

This is why the last word of the chapter is not about effort. A journey can be long and the person on it can take wrong turns, carry things they should have set down, climb things they should have left alone. The verse says that the one they were walking toward was carrying their provisions the whole way.

In this game the embrace, the garland, the river and the friends on the bank are the game's own picture of a soul coming home; the scene is fiction. The promise that He carries what His devotees lack and preserves what they have is the Gita's, and this is the verse that makes it.
wisdom.embrace.source: Bhagavad-gita 9.22 · told here in plain words, not the verse itself. The licensed translation, with its edition, goes here after the panel approves it.
wisdom.embrace.verse: Those who think of Me and of nothing else, and worship Me with constancy: what they lack, I bring to them, and what they have, I keep safe.
wisdom.give.meaning: Work done as an offering frees. Work done for oneself binds.
wisdom.give.more:
The word the verse turns on is yajna, usually translated as sacrifice. In the Gita it does not mean giving something up so much as giving something over: doing an action as an offering, for Vishnu, for the whole, rather than for oneself alone. Krishna says that work done in this spirit does not bind the one who does it, and that every other kind of work does. Then He tells Arjuna to work anyway, as an offering, free of clinging.

This matters because the alternative, doing nothing, is not on offer. Everyone acts. A can of water is carried whether it is carried to a shop shelf or to a dry fountain. The verse says the action itself does not decide whether it frees or binds; what it is for decides that. The same walk, with the same weight on the shoulder, can be two different things.

The tradition pictures the difference as planting. An act for oneself drops a seed that will fruit as more wanting; an act given over drops a seed of a different kind. Nobody sees either seed at the time. The verse is not asking for a feeling of piety while working. It asks for a change of address on the parcel.

Carrying water for someone else is the oldest action in this game, and it comes back whenever something is asked that costs a little. The street, the fountain and the shopkeeper are the game's fiction. The teaching that work done as an offering frees and work done for oneself binds is the Gita's, and this is the verse.
wisdom.give.source: Bhagavad-gita 3.9 · told here in plain words, not the verse itself. The licensed translation, with its edition, goes here after the panel approves it.
wisdom.give.verse: Work done as an offering sets a person free; any other work binds them to this world. So do what is yours to do as an offering, and act without clinging to the result.
wisdom.melody.meaning: Give up all other paths and surrender to Me; I will free you from all reactions. Do not fear.
wisdom.melody.more:
This is the Gita's final instruction, and the tradition treats it as the heart of the book. Krishna has spent seventeen chapters describing paths: duty, knowledge, discipline, work without attachment. Here He says: set all of that aside and come to Me alone. I will free you from every consequence of what you have done. Do not fear.

Surrender in this verse is not defeat, and not giving up on anything worth having. It is the moment a person stops carrying the whole weight alone. Everything that was being managed, earned, defended and counted is handed over to someone who was already holding it. The last words are the ones the tradition dwells on. The verse does not say, do better. It says, do not fear.

The sound heard low in the shrine, and again here, is the maha-mantra, the great chant:

Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.

It is the names of Krishna, of Rama and of Hara, His own energy, sung as a call to be taken back into His company. It is not a password, a formula or a power, and in this game it is never a collectible.

The Song is the game's way of picturing the pull of Krishna's flute; the tradition describes this in the Tenth Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam. The Veena, the tower and the dawn are fiction. The verse, and the promise in it, are the Gita's own.
wisdom.melody.source: Bhagavad-gita 18.66 · told here in plain words, not the verse itself. The licensed translation, with its edition, goes here after the panel approves it.
wisdom.melody.verse: Give up every other path and take shelter in Me alone. I will free you from all the consequences of your actions; do not fear.
wisdom.shrine_water.meaning: A leaf, a flower, fruit or water offered with love is accepted. What is offered matters less than the love it is offered with.
wisdom.shrine_water.more:
This is one of the gentlest verses in the Bhagavad-gita. Krishna has been speaking about devotion, and here He says what it costs: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, some water. Not a feast, not gold, not a great deed. Whatever is at hand, if it is offered with love, He accepts, and the verse adds that it is the love He takes, from someone whose heart has grown clear.

The tradition reads this as a door that is never shut. A person with nothing can offer water; a child can offer a leaf. Nobody is priced out, nobody needs permission, and the size of the gift says nothing about how it is received. What matters is the direction of the offering, which is the same point the Gita makes about work: the act is small, the turning is everything.

The lamp in a shrine room is kept burning with exactly this: water, oil, a flower, a little attention each day. It looks like nothing from outside. From inside the tradition it is a conversation that has been going on for a very long time, and anyone can join it with what they happen to be carrying.

Madhuri, her shrine room and the lamp are the game's own fiction; so is the basin and what is seen in it. The verse, and the idea that a leaf or a flower or water offered with love is accepted, are the Gita's. The chant heard low in the shrine is the maha-mantra, a real chant of the tradition, written out in another card.
wisdom.shrine_water.source: Bhagavad-gita 9.26 · told here in plain words, not the verse itself. The licensed translation, with its edition, goes here after the panel approves it.
wisdom.shrine_water.verse: Whoever offers Me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water: that gift of love, from one whose heart is clear, I accept.
wisdom.take.meaning: Dwelling on things breeds attachment; attachment breeds desire; desire, when crossed, breeds anger. From there follow confusion, the loss of memory and the ruin of judgement.
wisdom.take.more:
These two verses describe a chain. It begins quietly, with attention. A person keeps turning something over in the mind, something the senses offered, and the turning becomes attachment. Attachment becomes desire: the thing must be had. Desire, when it is crossed, becomes anger. Anger clouds judgement; clouded judgement loses the thread of memory, the memory of who one is and what one was doing; and when that is gone, the intelligence that could have stepped back goes with it. The verses end with a person who is lost, not because of one act, but because of a chain nobody saw being forged.

What is striking is how ordinary every link is. Nothing here is a crime. It is a shortage, a worry, a reasonable precaution, a shop full of cans. A street gets its fences one link at a time, each one sensible on its own.

The verses are often read as a warning, but the Gita offers them as a description, the way a doctor describes how a cold becomes a fever. Knowing the chain is the beginning of being able to step out of it, at any link, because every link is a place where attention could turn elsewhere. The tradition's answer is not to stop wanting but to want something that does not run out.

Hollow Vale, the water shortage and the fences are the game's own picture of what the verses describe; they are fiction. The chain itself, from dwelling to attachment to desire to anger to forgetting, is the Gita's.
wisdom.take.source: Bhagavad-gita 2.62-63 · told here in plain words, not the verse itself. The licensed translation, with its edition, goes here after the panel approves it.
wisdom.take.verse: Dwelling on the things the senses offer, a person grows attached to them. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger; from anger, confusion; from confusion, the loss of memory; from that, the loss of good sense; and then the person is lost.
wisdom.whisper.meaning: The self is not the body it wears. It moves through bodies as a person moves through the ages of one life.
wisdom.whisper.more:
This is one of the first things Krishna says to Arjuna in the Bhagavad-gita. Arjuna is standing on a battlefield, unable to act, grieving for people who have not yet died. Krishna does not begin by telling him what to do. He begins by telling him what he is.

The body you had as a small child is gone. Every part of it has been replaced, and nobody mourns it, because the one who lived in it is still here. The tradition takes this everyday fact seriously. It says the self, the atma, is not the body at all but the one who looks out of it, and that the change called death is the same kind of change as growing up, only larger: the self sets down one body and takes up another. A person who understands this is not shaken when the body changes, in the way an adult is not shaken to have outgrown their childhood clothes.

Nothing in the verse asks anyone to stop caring for the body or for other people. It asks only that we not mistake the coat for the one wearing it.

In this game the Grove, its river, the feast and the bubble are the game's own picture of a soul at home and of the moment it looks elsewhere. They are fiction. The teaching that the self moves through bodies as a person moves through ages is the Gita's, and this verse is where it is first said.
wisdom.whisper.source: Bhagavad-gita 2.13 · told here in plain words, not the verse itself. The licensed translation, with its edition, goes here after the panel approves it.
wisdom.whisper.verse: As the one who lives in this body passes through childhood, youth and old age, so at death it passes into another body. One who knows this is not shaken by the change.
